title: The Dark Majority

A planet of deep water: PRIZE Most of the living space on this planet has never seen sunlight.
PRIZE Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface, but the surface is the smallest part of the story.
The average depth is close to 3,700 metres.
Sunlight gives up long before that.
By 200 metres there is too little of it for photosynthesis, and by 1,000 metres it is gone completely.
Everything below that line is the deep sea.
It holds roughly 90% of the ocean's volume.
PRIZE In other words, the typical place to live on Earth is cold, dark and pressed under kilometres of water.
Food falls from above: Almost nothing grows in the deep.
Most of its food arrives as marine snow: a slow drift of dead plankton, waste and dust from the sunlit water far above.
Only about 1% of what the surface produces ever lands on the seafloor.
Hydrothermal vents, discovered in 1977, run on chemistry instead of sunlight.
At the vents, water heated by magma emerges at up to 400 °C.
Bacteria feed on the minerals dissolved in it, and tube worms more than 2 metres long house the bacteria.
Ultimately, it is a food chain that starts with rock, not sunlight.
Light made by life: Where the sun stops, animals take over the job.
A survey off the California coast found that 76% of the animals observed in the water column could produce their own light.
It may be the most common form of communication on the planet.
The light is used to hunt, to hide and to find a mate.
In the dark, light is language.
Pressure: Pressure rises by one atmosphere every 10 metres.
At the bottom of the Challenger Deep, nearly 11 kilometres down, it passes 1,000 atmospheres.
The animals that live there do not resist the pressure so much as ignore it.
Their bodies are mostly water, which barely compresses, and their proteins are steadied by small molecules that keep them folding correctly.
The result is an environment that barely changes from one century to the next.
The Dark Majority: PRIZE We have barely looked at it.
LEAD Put simply: we cannot protect what we have never seen.
The map is mostly blank: Of our own seafloor, only about a quarter has been mapped at high resolution.
The rest is known from satellite estimates that blur anything smaller than a few kilometres.
People first reached the deepest point of the ocean in 1960.
Why it matters: The deep sea stores heat and carbon on a scale that shapes the climate of the whole planet.
It is also being considered for mining before it has been properly surveyed.
That is why the next decade of exploration matters more than the last century.
